summary: RFC 6374 defines packet loss and delay measurement for MPLS networks. This standards-track RFC specifies how to send and process out-of-band responses over a UDP/IP return path.

eli5.summary: A way for a measurement reply to come back by regular internet delivery instead of along the special path.

questions: mpls loss delay udp return path
what is the udp return object
how does mpls-pldm reply over udp
subtitle: A way for MPLS loss and delay measurement replies to come back over plain UDP/IP to a chosen address and port.

tldr.problem: MPLS loss and delay measurement (RFC 6374) has no way to deliver a Response to a particular node inside a multi-CPU router, or to a separate collector, or through firewalls.
tldr.mechanism: The querier adds a UDP Return Object (type 131) holding an IP address and UDP port to its Query, and the responder sends the Response there as a normal UDP/IP packet.
tldr.outcome: Responses can be steered to the right measurement process or collector, at the cost of supporting only one-way measurements on that return path.

facts.label: Rate needing extra care
facts.value: more than one packet per three seconds

today: RFC 7876 is a Proposed Standard from July 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends RFC 6374 without changing the rest of that protocol.

sections.title: Why a UDP Return Path
sections.content:
RFC 6374 defines Packet Loss and Delay Measurement for MPLS networks (MPLS-PLDM). A querier sends a Query and a responder sends back a Response. This RFC describes how an out-of-band Response can be delivered over UDP/IP.

The document gives several reasons. UDP may be needed for data-path management such as passing through firewalls, or for multiplexing when the querier and a collector are in different places and the collector gathers Responses from many responders. In a highly scaled Label Switching Router (LSR), a session may be off-loaded to a particular node, and a Response may arrive on any interface. RFC 6374 has no mechanism to deliver a Response to a particular node in a multi-CPU LSR.

Nothing else changes in the protocol. Delivery over an MPLS Associated Channel (RFC 5586) is unaffected.
sections.eli5: A big router has many little workers inside it. This lets the answer go straight to the right worker, instead of landing on the wrong desk.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
Unless configured otherwise, if a UDP Return Object (URO) is present in an MPLS-PLDM Query, the responder SHOULD reply to the IP address and UDP port in the URO. A querier MAY include several UROs, which tells the responder to send an identical Response to each address-port pair. A responder MAY be built or configured to send only one Response, in which case it MUST use the first URO it is able to use.

The procedures apply to unidirectional and bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs), including co-routed bidirectional LSPs and associated bidirectional LSPs made from a pair of unidirectional ones. They apply to both IP/MPLS and the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP).
sections.eli5: The asker writes one or more return addresses on the question. The answerer sends a copy of its reply to each one.

sections.title: The UDP Return Object
sections.content:
The URO is a TLV with an 8-bit URO Type and an 8-bit Length, followed by a 16-bit UDP-Destination-Port and an Address. The URO Type value is 131.

Length counts the rest of the object, which is the address size in bytes plus 2. It is 6 for an IPv4 address and 18 for an IPv6 address, so it serves both as the TLV parsing parameter and as the address family indicator.

The URO MUST NOT appear in a Response and MUST be ignored if it does. To avoid ambiguity, a Query with a URO MUST NOT carry the RFC 6374 Return Address TLV (TLV 1), and the return address MUST NOT be built from the Source Address TLV (TLV 130) for such a Query.
sections.eli5: The return-address label has a type, a size, a mailbox number and the address. The size also tells you which kind of address it is.

sections.title: Querier and Responder Procedures
sections.content:
When sending a Query, the querier MUST set the Control Code to "Out-of-band Response Requested" and MUST carry a URO. If it uses the UDP port to sort Responses by measurement type, it MUST use a different port for each type (delay, loss, and delay-loss combined). It MAY use several ports for the same type to reach the right management process in the LSR.

On receiving such a Query with a URO, the responder SHOULD send the Response to that address and port. If the URO is missing, the Query MUST NOT be processed further. On a unidirectional LSP it SHOULD be dropped. On a bidirectional LSP the Response Control Code SHOULD be 0x1C, "Error - Invalid Message", sent over the reverse LSP. The operator SHOULD be told through the management system, with precautions against overloading error reporting.

In the Response, the destination address and port are copied from the URO, while the source address and port are left to the responder. If URO(s) were given for only one address family and no return path of that family exists, the Query MUST be discarded. A responder set to send one Response MAY look for the first URO it has a path for.

The Response has no Associated Channel Header, since the UDP port and the session identifier in the RFC 6374 message bind it to the Query. On an IP return path only one-way delay or one-way loss can be measured, and timestamps 3 and 4 MUST be zero. A Response received over UDP when none was requested SHOULD be dropped and reported.
sections.eli5: The asker must say where to reply. If the return address is missing or cannot be reached, the answerer does not reply that way and tells the network operator.

sections.title: Congestion and Manageability
sections.content:
The protocol MUST be run according to RFC 5405. For rates above one packet per three seconds, operators need to provision the MPLS path and any IP return path so there is a negligible chance of causing congestion. If many Responses are lost, the querier MUST reduce its sending rate. Operators should also keep Response packets from leaking out of the network domain.

The manageability considerations in Section 7 of RFC 6374 apply. A configured UDP/IP return path can be used instead of signaling, in which case the URO MAY be omitted.
sections.eli5: If lots of answers get lost, the asker must ask less often, so it does not clog the roads.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MPLS-PLDM is not intended for the public Internet, but for well-managed private and service provider networks. The security considerations in Section 8 of RFC 6374 apply, and access-control lists and firewalls can strengthen the cryptographic measures.

To keep the protocol from becoming a reflection attack vector, the operator should make sure the address in the URO belongs to a system that expects to receive PLDM Responses. The RFC says there is no additional exposure of information to pervasive monitoring systems observing monitored LSPs.
sections.eli5: Someone could write a stranger's address on the return label to flood them with mail. Operators must make sure the address belongs to a real receiver.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned a new optional TLV type, code 131 with the description "UDP Return", in the "MPLS Loss/Delay Measurement TLV Object" registry within the "Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) Parameters" registry set.
sections.eli5: The number 131 was reserved in an official list so that everybody means the same thing by it.
